To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the majority of amnestic MCL/DAT cases in the ADNI cohort had a coincident pathology with AD (AD+), 2) biomarkers (clinical, neuropsychological, CSF and neuroimaging) can be used to predict the presence of coincident AD+DLB, AD+MTL and AD+vascular, and 3) the presence of coincidental AD+DLB was associated with a more severe dysexcutive cognitive profile and

coincident dementia with Lewy body pathology can be predicted by hallucinations and occipital hypometabolism and that coincident medial temporal lobe pathologies can be predicted by hippocampal volume.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new approach to the development of a novel biomarker for the development of a clinical and multimodal biomaker correlates of ADNI.
the study of biomarkers for Alzheimer’s disease and related neurodegenerative diseases.
the development of a new method for identifying and quantifying the presence of coincident pathologic processes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presence or absence of coincident pathology does not affect the clinical or biomarker profile of AD.
all patients with a clinical AD diagnosis had some form of AD pathology.

all patients had AD, but that the clinical diagnosis of DAT and MCI-AD were not specific for AD, and that the neuropathological diagnosis of AD was not specific for the clinical diagnosis of dementia.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
coincident DLB is associated with a more severe clinical presentation and with occipital hypometabolism.
coincident pathologies are more common than expected, but can be accurately predicted with biomarkers.
coincident pathologies are common in autopsy series of patients with a clinical dementia diagnosis.
The main takeaway from our work is that

biomarkers can be used as a tool to identify patients with a specific neuropathology, which is useful for the design of clinical trials and for the study of the natural history of different neuropathologies.
biomarkers are not interchangeable and should not be used as proxies for each other.
the neuropathological substrata of dementia are not mutually exclusive and that the use of biomarkers may help identify the neuropathological basis of dementia in individual patients.
